20477-the-book-of-ballads-edited-by-bon-:
The Book of Ballads edited by Bon Gaultier collects the comic and romantic ballads written for Blackwood's Magazine. Bon Gaultier was the shared pen name behind the pieces. The editor's memoir tells how he and William Edmonstoune Aytoun came together in the work.

Aytoun was born on June 21, 1813, three years before his partner. He was already known as a writer in Blackwood's when the two joined forces. For two or three years they wrote together in literature. Their ballads parodied famous poems and mocked public figures, and readers of the magazine prized their polish and bite.
29281-remarks-concerning-stones-said-to-:
Edward King, fellow of the Royal Society and the Society of Antiquaries, published these remarks in London in 1796. King attempts to explain stones reported falling in Tuscany on June 16, 1794, and to show traces of similar events in the highest ages of antiquity. He works from manuscript accounts sent by Sir Charles Blagden.

King also inserts an account of an extraordinary hailstone that dropped with many others in Cornwall on October 20, 1791. His argument treats falling stones as real phenomena with ancient parallels, before meteoritics became a science. Readers get an early scientific inquiry into meteorites, curious and learned, from a time when stones from the sky still needed explaining.
3095-the-lady-of-the-shroud:
Bram Stoker wrote The Lady of the Shroud in 1909, after Dracula, The Jewel of Seven Stars, and The Mystery of the Sea, dedicating it to his friend the Comtesse de Guerbel. The novel opens with a clipping from the Journal of Occultism. It reports a strange Adriatic story from the Italia steamer Victorine, passing the Spear of Ivan on the coast of the Blue Mountains shortly before midnight. The tale follows Rupert Saint Leger, heir to a Balkan principality, and a mysterious woman in a shroud who visits his castle by night.

A Scottish auntie, shutting a window against cold air, calls it a fearsome night for her poor old aunt. Stoker mixes romance, politics, and the supernatural in a Balkan setting, and the novel rewards readers who enjoy his later, less famous fiction.
32082-a-rent-in-a-cloud:
Charles Lever's novel opens at the White Horse at Coblentz, in a room looking over the rapid Rhine. Two young Englishmen lounge at a window of the Weissen Ross, smoking cigars in a sunset tint, wearing the air of boredom that belongs to youth at its most enjoyable. They met only a few days before, on an Antwerp steamer, in a picture gallery, and side by side at a Brussels table d'hote.

Drifting into the intimacy that very young men call friendship, they agree to travel together. Neither cares much in what direction. Calvert must return to India in October to join his regiment, while Loyd must be in England about the same time, having just been called to the bar. Loyd asks if Calvert likes soldiering, and Calvert answers that he hates it. Readers get a Rhine travel tale of two young men at a crossroads.
33501-the-book-of-gud:
Dan Spain and Harold Hersey's Book of Gud, from Main Street magazine of July 1929, centers on a forgotten god and his adventures the day after eternity. The book invites readers to dip in anywhere, and it suggests chapter sixteen as a sample. Its first chapter opens one Sunday afternoon, as the tale's strange, comic premise unfolds.

The novel's humor lies in its bold, satirical fancy, where a forgotten god must find his way in a world that has moved on. Its tone is light and irreverent, suited to readers who enjoy comic fantasy. For fans of odd, early pulp novels, The Book of Gud offers a curious, entertaining tale of divinity down on its luck.
33829-the-nightriders-feud:
Walter C. McConnell writes a western feud novel in this 1912 book. John Redmond the second, newly graduated with high honors from a New York college and ready to set the world on fire with brilliance, feels instead the call of the wild. That call has long held his heart. Since earliest recollection his soul has longed for the wild western country, and he determines to seek gold or coal in great western mountains where others passed over immense hidden wealth.

Trained as an engineer, Redmond believes his skill will reveal what others missed, and that the wealth was placed there for his discovery. The train carries him homeward while his future flits through his study-laden brain. From that ambitious start, the novel moves into mountain feuds, nightriders, and the clash between eastern education and western violence. Readers of early western fiction will enjoy its earnest, romantic hero.
7559-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-t:
The memoirs of the court of St. Cloud, Napoleon's palace outside Paris, are gathered here in quotations and images. A gentleman at Paris opens the entries. Beside him is a stranger to remorse and repentance as well as to honor, and a woman accused of fanaticism because she refused to cohabit with her husband. All his creditors, denounced and executed, shows the Terror's shadow still falling.

Bonaparte and his wife go now every morning to hear Mass, yet Bonaparte dreads the liberty of the press more than all other things. Priests are to be proscribed as criminals, injustice is supported by violence, and courtiers bow to charlatanism as if it were sublimity. The volume is Napoleon's court seen from inside: confident, obstinate, and, as one entry says, ignorant in its certainty.
britannica-1911-abraham-ibn-daud:
Abraham ibn Daud receives a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Ibn Daud, a Jewish historiographer and philosopher of Toledo who lived about 1110 to 1180, wrote the Book of Tradition, a chronicle down to 1161 defending the traditional record.

Medieval facts of value fill that history, later turned into Latin by Génébrad. His philosophy came in an Arabic work known by its Hebrew title 'Emunah Ramah, Sublime Faith. Among the first Jewish scholastics to take up Aristotle's system, where his forerunners leaned Neo-Platonist, he fed much into Maimonides, the entry closes. One short notice thus joins the chronicler and the thinker in a single Spanish figure.
britannica-1911-alp-arslan-mahommed-ben-:
Alp Arslan, or Mahommed ben Da'ud (1029–1072), was the second sultan of the Seljuk dynasty in Persia and great-grandson of Seljuk, its founder. He took the name Mahommed on embracing Islam, and his surname, meaning a valiant lion, marked his military prowess. He succeeded his father as ruler of Khorasan in 1059 and his uncle as sultan in 1063, becoming sole monarch of Persia from the Oxus to the Tigris.

Aided by his vizier Nizām ul-Mulk, Alp Arslan consolidated his empire and named his son Malik Shah as heir. He plundered Caesarea in Cappadocia, subdued Armenia and Georgia by 1064, and from 1068 campaigned against the Roman empire of Romanus Diogenes. The entry closes with his death on 15 December 1072, from an assassin's dagger wound received after a captured enemy was brought before him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adolphe-perra:
Adolphe Perraud was a cardinal and academician born at Lyons on 7 February 1828, who died on 18 February 1906. He shone at the lycees Henri IV and St. Louis, entered the Ecole Normale under Gratry's influence, won the history fellowship in 1850, and taught two years at Angers. In 1852 he left teaching for the priesthood and joined the Oratory in Paris, then being reorganized by Gratry and Petetot.

Ordained in 1855 after a stay at Rome, he became history professor and religion prefect at St. Lo's petit seminaire, while devoting himself to preaching. In 1860 he visited Ireland and wrote Contemporary Ireland in 1862. In 1866 the Sorbonne made him its ecclesiastical history professor, treating Protestantism brilliantly. Made Bishop of Autun in 1874 despite liberal tendencies, he served working men closely, preaching the funeral sermon after the Montceau mining disaster killed twenty-two.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-domin:
Antoine-Dominique Magaud, a French painter born at Marseilles in 1817, led the city's art school so well that he was called its second founder. Trained in Paris under Léon Cogniet, he painted portraits and landscapes, yet his real strength lay in large decorative work. Across Marseilles he adorned the Chamber of Commerce, the library, the prefecture, and grand hotels.

His masterpiece was a historical gallery for the Marseilles Religious Association, with fifteen great canvases and a vast ceiling. Its theme glorified Christian civilization, with religion shown as the source that inspires learning, science, and art. Side walls carried scenes from philosophy to the early martyrs, and the entry ranks Magaud among the finest decorative painters of his city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augustus-theb:
Augustus Thebaud was a Jesuit educator and publicist born at Nantes in France in 1807, who died at Fordham in New York in 1885. His parents, a merchant and his pious wife, married during the Terror by a loyal priest, and their children received France's best religious schooling then. Thebaud studied at Nantes, was ordained, and worked three years in parishes before entering the Society of Jesus in Italy in 1835. He then studied science at the Sorbonne under Ampere.

He reached the United States in December 1838. He took the chemistry chair at St Mary's College in Kentucky, becoming its rector in 1846. That year the Jesuits moved to St John's College, Fordham, where Thebaud served as first Jesuit president from 1846 to 1851 and again from 1860 to 1863. Between and after those terms he pastored St Joseph's at Troy. From 1875 until his death he wrote his reminiscences in three volumes, energetic even in old age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fraud:
Fraud, in the common acceptation, is an act or course of deceit deliberately practised to gain a wrong and unfair advantage. Its meaning is narrower than deceit, which covers concealment or perversion of truth to mislead. War stratagems to deceive an enemy are not morally wrong, yet even in wartime fraud against an enemy would be wrong. Fraud offends not only sincerity but justice, and justice is owed even to enemies.

If fraud leads a party into a mistake about the substance of a contract, the contract is null and void. A dealer who sells coloured glass as a valuable ruby for a large sum has no true agreement, since the buyer wished a precious stone and was offered glass. If the fraudulent mistake concerns only an accidental point that did not induce the bargain, the contract stands and need not be set aside.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henri-faraud:
Oblate bishop Henri Faraud, born at Gigondas in 1823, carried the faith to Canada's far north as first Vicar Apostolic of Athabasca-Mackenzie. Sent to America while still in minor orders, ordained at St. Boniface in 1847, he replaced Laflèche at Ile-à-la-Crosse, founded Lake Athabasca mission in 1851, and visited Great Slave Lake and Peace River country no missionary had reached.

Named vicar apostolic in May 1862, he learned of it only in July 1863, so deep was his isolation, and was consecrated Bishop of Anemour in November 1864. For twenty-five years he founded posts to the Frozen Ocean and the Liard River, attended the 1889 St. Boniface council, and died at St. Boniface in 1890, too infirm to return north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-franco:
Joseph-François Michaud was a French historian best known for his History of the Crusades. Born at Albens in Savoy in 1767, he worked in publishing at Lyons and journalism in Paris. There he defended the royal cause during the Revolution and later spent time in prison for criticizing Napoleon. In 1808 he turned from politics to literature.

His History of the Crusades, first issued from 1812 to 1817, helped restore the Middle Ages to honor in French letters. Later scholars found its facts thin and its romance at times false. With his brother he founded the Biographie Universelle, and in 1830 he traveled to the Holy Land to give his history truer local color.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-victor-:
Louis Victor Emile Bougaud was Bishop of Laval, born at Dijon in 1823 and dead at Laval in 1888. Schooled at Autun under the future Cardinal Pitra, he studied theology at Dijon and Paris, was ordained in 1846, and taught church history at Dijon seminary.

As chaplain of the Visitation convent he wrote lives of St. Benignus and St. Chantal. As vicar-general under Dupanloup at Orleans he wrote lives of St. Monica, Margaret Mary, and Vincent de Paul, plus his five-volume apology, Christianity and the Present Age. Made Bishop of Laval in 1886, he preached and wrote with sympathy for his age, hoping the Church would win it without yielding doctrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-de-cala:
Pedro de Calatayud was a Jesuit missionary born in Navarre on 1 August 1689, dead at Bologna on 27 February 1773. He joined the Society of Jesus in 1710. Madrid's Academy holds an account of his Bilbao mission. He was Master in Theology and left many theological works.

Among them are The Flame of Holy Love for the Sacred Heart and Various Sentences from Scripture for Missionaries' Use. Others are Practice of a Sweet and Reasonable Christian Life, Regrets of a Contrite Heart, and Practical Doctrines for Explanation on the Missions, famous. Further works are his Doctrinal Compendium, an extended Pinamonti edition, his Practical Catechism, and his Spiritual Exercises for Priests and Ordinandi. One proposition of the last, on restitution by a negligent priest, drew criticism. He also wrote Practical and Doctrinal Methods for Religious. He published many pamphlets and brochures. Living at the Society's suppression, he was expelled from Spain and died after.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-cloud:
Saint Cloud is a suffragan of the Archdiocese of St Paul, Minnesota, comprising sixteen counties in Minnesota, an area of 12,251 square miles. The bishop resides in St Cloud. In 1680 Father Hennepin visited the Indians at Mille Lacs, and for 170 years no other priest came. In 1851, when this part of Minnesota opened to settlers, the diocese's history begins.

In 1852 Francis Pierz came from Lake Superior missions to labour among the Chippewa. Finding the country fit for farming, he announced it in Catholic German papers, causing large German Catholic immigration. In 1856 Bishop Cretin sent three Benedictines, who settled near present St Cloud and built a log house and chapel. In 1857 they put up a college and started a school for five pupils. Moving to St John's Lake, they established a college and monastery in 1866.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-carlos-de:
San Carlos de Ancud, the southernmost diocese of Chile, stretches from the River Cautín in the north to Cape Horn. It takes in Valdivia, Llanquihue, and Chiloé, part of Cautín, and the Magallanes territory. It spans over 77,220 square miles with 371,856 people, of whom 356,267 are Catholics. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia gives a statistical portrait of a far-southern church.

Ancud itself holds only 3,500 people, while Valdivia counts 15,000, Puerto Montt 5,500, Osorno 7,600, and Punta Arenas 12,300. Forty-eight parishes serve the diocese, with a cathedral chapter of dean, archdeacon, doctoral, and canon. A Jesuit-run seminary holds 106 students, and sixty-nine secular and eighty-six regular priests serve thirty houses of male religious. The entry suits readers mapping Catholic life at the world's southern edge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-of-cram:
Simon of Cramaud, cardinal born near Rochechouart in the diocese of Limoges before 1360, died at Poitiers on 14 December 1422. He studied law at Orléans and won an excellent name as a canonist. In 1382 he became Bishop of Agen, moving to Béziers in 1383 and Poitiers in 1385. He never held Sens, named in 1390, but became titular Patriarch of Alexandria and administrator of Avignon.

A leading figure in the Great Schism, he championed Clement VII at first, then turned decided opponent of his successor Benedict XIII. At national synods and on diplomatic missions he pressed for withdrawal from Benedict's obedience. At Pisa in 1409 he presided over the council that deposed both Gregory XII and Benedict XIII and elected Alexander V. At Constance he helped carry an unusual election rule giving votes to national delegates beside cardinals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-talmud:
The Talmud began as a word for doctrine or study. It comes from a Hebrew verb meaning to teach. In its special sense it means the justification and explanation of Halakhoth. Halakhoth are the religious and legal norms governing conduct. When Jehuda's third-century Mishna became the chief study, Talmud meant chiefly its discussions. Finally it meant the Mishna plus those discussions, called Gemara, or completion.

Since Ezra, Jewish communal life rested on fixed law from the Pentateuch. Nothing might be added to that law or changed. Yet changing life demanded new rulings, decreed case by case and handed down orally. A ruling of immemorial age counted as law given to Moses on Sinai. Orthodox faith still holds that Moses received oral law with the written one. The entry then follows the Talmud's growth and printed editions, closing with a full bibliography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theophile-ray:
Jesuit writer Théophile Raynaud, theologian of vast output, is the scholar sketched here. Born at Sospello near Nice on 15 November 1583, he died at Lyons on 31 October 1663. He joined the Society of Jesus on 21 November 1602, taught grammar and letters at Avignon, then philosophy and theology at Lyons and for a time at Rome. Zeal for souls matched broad learning.

Ninety-two separate works cover nearly all theology, though his style runs prolix and at times obscure, and his polemics indulge satire and invective. His collected works, revised by himself near death, appeared under fellow Jesuit John Bertet in nineteen volumes at Lyons in 1665. A twentieth volume, Apopompaeus or scapegoat, holding works he had left out, came from an unnamed editor at Cracow in 1669 and drew Index condemnation.
doe-osti-3017673-demonstration-trials-of:
Marco Pritoni of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory was the technical contact, with Thomas Mills of PACE AI as partner contact, for this CRADA final report dated December 28, 2025. The agreement, FP00016419, ran demonstration trials of the PACE5 edge node. The device is an artificial intelligence suite that works at the building edge and in the cloud to manage energy use.

Trials ran at FLEXLAB, the laboratory's building test facility. The prototype was installed and cycled through baseline periods and active test periods. The goal was to test response to dynamic price signals: shedding demand when prices rise, and taking on load when they fall. Fault detection and microgrid monitoring were also demonstrated. Results showed the prototype did perform demand shed and take as prices changed. Funding totaled 376,170 dollars, routed largely through the California Energy Commission. The short filing records a working trial, with findings tabled inside.
doe-osti-3376257-demonstration-trials-of:
A CRADA final report dated December 28, 2025, closes demo trials of an AI edge and cloud suite built by PACE AI with Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Marco Pritoni was the lab contact. Thomas Mills served for the firm. The suite steers building gear from a small on-site node, with cloud help behind it. It chases three jobs: shed load on price spikes, take load when power is cheap, and flag faults early. A microgrid watch mode rides along.

The PACE5 edge node went into the lab's FLEXLAB test cells. Staff ran matched spans of plain and AI-led days. On the median day, energy use fell from 10.01 to 9.19 kilowatt-hours. That is a saving of 0.82 kilowatt-hours a day under test terms. Cost and comfort marks sit in the same table. The report is candid that no formal publication was planned for this work under the CRADA terms.
govdocs-archive_org-propaganda-the-forma:
Jacques Ellul, the French sociologist, published Propaganda: The Formation of Men's Attitudes in French in 1962, and it reached English readers in 1965. Ellul argues that propaganda is not a few posters or speeches. It is a whole condition of modern life.

Governments, parties, advertisers, and media together shape what whole societies think, often without any single liar in charge. Ellul insists that educated people are propaganda's best targets, not its safeguards. The book became a classic of media theory, and its cold view of mass persuasion still unsettles readers who meet it today.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_cybervault_HR_494:
H. R. 4943 carries a long name, the Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act, shortened to the CLOUD Act. A National Security Archive cyber brief explains what the act does. It lets American law enforcement serve warrants and subpoenas for data stored on servers anywhere in the world. The one condition is that the company holding the data is based in the United States.

That rule settled a fight that had reached the Supreme Court, over whether a warrant could reach email stored in another country. Where data physically sits no longer controls the answer; who holds it does. For readers, the brief is a plain-language guide to a law that quietly reshaped privacy and policing across borders. It remains a reference point in every later argument over government access to cloud data.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-the-co:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of the Court of St. Cloud selects from an account credited to a gentleman at Paris, covering Napoleon's court at Saint-Cloud. David Widger's extracts run alphabetically, sentence by sentence, through the manners and fears of the new empire.

Bonaparte and his wife go every morning to hear Mass, one entry reports, yet Bonaparte dreads the liberty of the press more than all else. Priests are to be proscribed as criminals, creditors are denounced and executed, and a figure called the Chevalier of the Guillotine appears. Power forcing the law is the refrain of the whole bitter selection.
the-lady-of-the-shroud:
Bram Stoker, author of Dracula, published this novel with Rider and Company of London in 1909, dedicating it to his old friend the Comtesse de Guerbel, the actress Genevieve Ward. It opens not with a narrator but with a clipping from The Journal of Occultism, mid-January 1907, reporting a strange story from the Adriatic. On the night of the ninth, the steamship Victorine passed the Spear of Ivan on the coast of the Blue Mountains a little before midnight.

The lookout called the captain to a tiny floating light close inshore, where ships had once hugged the coast so closely that Lloyd's had warned of the risk. Captain Mirolani slowed the engines and edged in to investigate possible distress, joined by his officers and by a passenger, Mr. Peter Caulfield, known for reports of spiritual phenomena. Stoker frames his shrouded lady as a documented mystery, attested by signatures.
